lead: IEEE 802.15.4 is a low-rate, low-power wireless standard for the physical and MAC layers of small sensor and control networks. It exists because Wi-Fi and Bluetooth cost too much power for battery nodes that send few bytes. It gives a shared radio foundation under ZigBee, 6LoWPAN and WirelessHART, so home sensors, smart meters and factory monitors can interoperate. Some syllabi call it LR-WPAN, for low-rate wireless personal area network. It is the shared radio layer under ZigBee and 6LoWPAN; the next chapters build the upper layers on it.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 wireless sensor networks and Chapter 3.1 on layered protocol models.

sections.h3: Physical layer: bands, rates and channels

blocks.text: IEEE 802.15.4 defines the physical layer, or PHY, and the medium access control layer, or MAC. The PHY turns bits into radio signals. The MAC decides when a node may transmit. The standard is low rate and low power: a node can sleep most of the time and wake to send a few bytes.

The PHY uses three licence-free bands. At 868 MHz it has one channel, binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) and 20 kbps. At 915 MHz it has ten channels, BPSK and 40 kbps. At 2.4 GHz it has sixteen channels numbered 11 to 26, offset quadrature phase-shift keying (OQPSK) and 250 kbps. The 2.4 GHz band is worldwide and gives the highest rate, so most consumer nodes use it. A PHY frame has a 4-byte preamble, a 1-byte start-of-frame delimiter (SFD), a 1-byte length field and a PSDU, the physical service data unit. The PSDU is the MAC frame and can be up to 127 bytes. Its last 2 bytes are the frame check sequence (FCS), a CRC that detects bit errors. The PHY adds 6 bytes before the PSDU: a 4-byte preamble, a 1-byte SFD and a 1-byte length field.

sections.h3: MAC layer: CSMA/CA, beacons and time slots

blocks.text: The MAC uses carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA). A node that has a frame first listens to the channel. If the channel is busy, it waits. If free, it waits a random backoff and listens again. It sends only when the channel is still free. The receiver returns an acknowledgement (ACK) frame. If the ACK does not arrive, the sender retries.

In beacon-enabled mode a coordinator sends a beacon at fixed intervals. The time between beacons is the beacon interval, BI. The active part is the superframe duration, SD. The rest is inactive, when nodes may sleep. The active superframe has 16 equal slots. The contention access period (CAP) uses CSMA/CA. The contention-free period (CFP) has guaranteed time slots (GTS), up to seven, for urgent or periodic data.

blocks.where: BI is the beacon interval; SD is the superframe duration; BO is the beacon order; SO is the superframe order; aBaseSuperframeDuration is the smallest superframe length in symbols; SO ≤ BO.

blocks.text: The duty cycle is SD / BI = 2<sup>SO−BO</sup> (two raised to the power SO − BO). When SO = 3 and BO = 6 this gives 2<sup>−3</sup> = 1/8 = 12.5 %. A small duty cycle saves battery but gives fewer active slots. In non-beacon mode there is no superframe. Nodes use unslotted CSMA/CA and may sleep on their own schedule. This is simpler but has no guaranteed slots. Beacons also carry network information and wake sleeping nodes.

An 802.15.4 network has three topologies. In a star, every device talks only to one coordinator. It is simple and predictable. In peer-to-peer, any device can talk to any other device in range; this allows mesh routing above 802.15.4. In a cluster tree, coordinators form a tree, and devices join the nearest parent. ZigBee uses these topologies on top of 802.15.4; see Chapter 3.3.

Each device has a 64-bit extended address, a unique hardware address. A coordinator can also give a 16-bit short address, which saves frame space. A frame carries source and destination address fields, so short addresses reduce overhead.

There are four MAC frame types. A beacon frame starts a superframe and advertises the network. A data frame carries payload. An ACK frame confirms receipt. A MAC command frame carries control messages such as association requests. Each frame has a frame control field, sequence number, addressing fields, payload and FCS. The maximum PSDU is 127 bytes, so payload is small; 6LoWPAN compresses IPv6 headers to fit; see Chapter 3.5.

figure.caption: The worked example as one chain: the 127-byte PSDU plus the 6 bytes the PHY adds gives 133 bytes on air, which is 1064 bits and takes 4.256 ms at 250 kbps.

spec.title: On-air time of a 127-byte PSDU at 250 kbps
spec.aria: A flow from a 127-byte PSDU and the 6 bytes of PHY overhead (4-byte preamble, 1-byte SFD, 1-byte length) to 133 bytes on air, then 133 times 8 equals 1064 bits, then 1064 divided by 250000 bits per second equals 4.256 milliseconds.

examples.question: An 802.15.4 data frame has a 127-byte PSDU. It is sent at 250 kbps. What is the total time on air including the 4-byte preamble, 1-byte SFD and 1-byte length? Ignore inter-frame spacing.
steps: PHY overhead = 4 B preamble + 1 B SFD + 1 B length = 6 B.
examples.answer: The total time on air is 4.256 ms for 133 bytes.
examples.check:
psdu = 127
overhead = 4 + 1 + 1
total = psdu + overhead
rate = 250000
time_ms = total * 8 / rate * 1000
print(total)
print(round(time_ms, 3))

traps: Do not add the 4-byte preamble, 1-byte SFD and 1-byte length to the 127-byte PSDU and call the result the MAC frame; 127 B is the PSDU, and the PHY adds 6 B.
Do not mix beacon-enabled and non-beacon CSMA/CA: beacon-enabled networks can use CAP and CFP with GTS; non-beacon networks have no superframe.
Do not treat the 16-bit short address as globally unique; it is assigned by a coordinator, while the 64-bit extended address is unique.
Do not use the 2.4 GHz rate of 250 kbps for the 868 MHz band; that band runs at 20 kbps.
Do not say 802.15.4 is the whole IoT stack; it is only PHY and MAC, and ZigBee or 6LoWPAN adds upper layers.

quiz.q: Which bands and data rates does IEEE 802.15.4 define?
quiz.a: 868 MHz at 20 kbps, 915 MHz at 40 kbps, and 2.4 GHz at 250 kbps.

quiz.q: Why does 802.15.4 use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?
quiz.a: Wireless nodes cannot detect collisions reliably while transmitting because their own signal masks others, so they avoid collisions by listening and random backoff, then use ACK.

quiz.q: Name the four MAC frame types in IEEE 802.15.4.
quiz.a: Beacon frame, data frame, ACK frame and MAC command frame.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a 16-bit short address and a 64-bit extended address?
quiz.a: The 64-bit extended address is a unique hardware address; the 16-bit short address is assigned by a coordinator to save frame space.

quiz.q: A 50-byte PSDU is sent at 250 kbps. Find the total on-air time with a 4-byte preamble, 1-byte SFD and 1-byte length; ignore inter-frame spacing.
quiz.a: Total bytes = 50 + 6 = 56 B. Total bits = 56 × 8 = 448 bits. Time = 448 / 250000 = 0.001792 s = 1.792 ms.

quiz.q: A beacon-enabled network has BO = 6 and SO = 3. Find the duty cycle and explain its effect on battery life.
quiz.a: Duty cycle = 2^(SO−BO) = 2^(3−6) = 1/8 = 12.5%. The node sleeps 87.5% of the beacon interval, saving battery but giving fewer active slots.

quiz.q: Why does a 127-byte PSDU limit IPv6, and what layer fixes it?
quiz.a: An IPv6 header is 40 B. Inside a 127-B PSDU the MAC header and 2-B FCS already take up to about 27 B, so well under 87 B (roughly 60 B) remains for transport and application data. That tight budget is why 6LoWPAN compresses headers and fragments.

beyond: Not for the exam. IEEE 802.15.4 is the base of Thread, a newer IPv6 mesh for homes, and of ZigBee PRO networks. Chip vendors sell 802.15.4 radios inside systems-on-chip with ARM cores, so a sensor node can run the MAC in hardware and sleep at microamp levels. Research extends it with energy harvesting, channel hopping and deterministic scheduling for industrial loops. Search for "IEEE 802.15.4e TSCH" and "Thread protocol" to go further.
